job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Marco Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at work by 7:30 at a family-run building supplies wholesaler, where I'm the accounts clerk. I studied business administration and started in August. I send invoices, chase unpaid accounts and reconcile the till with the bank. On Sundays I'm at church, and then lunch with my girlfriend Ola's family. I rent a bedroom in a house with two other men from the warehouse, and I leave early on Fridays to play five-a-side football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good. A business like ours runs on people who know each other, and no program is going to know that Mr Dabrowski pays on the fifteenth. I'd say that at work, at church and at the football pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm all right. I have a steady job, the owner likes me, and the hardware business doesn't vanish. But I have a debt of about twenty thousand and almost nothing saved. Ola and I want to marry in two years and I don't see how I pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, learn the stock system better and ask the owner, Mr Nowak, whether I can take over the credit control side. I'd add up our wedding costs honestly, maybe plan for a small one. I'd keep clear of AI. I don't trust something that I can't ask a person about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, apart from the money. Work feels like a place where I belong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the wedding costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make it smaller. Ola's mother has already said she'll do the food. We'd have it at the parish hall, not a restaurant. I'd rather start married with no new debt than have a big photo album.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust something you can't ask a person about. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person can say, I made a mistake. A program just gives an answer, and if it's wrong, who do I ring? When I was a student, my friend used one for an essay and it made up a source. That put me off for good.

say: A business like ours runs on people who **know each other**.
No program knows that Mr Dabrowski pays on the fifteenth.
think: My job is steady, but I owe about **twenty thousand** and have nearly no savings.
Ola and I want to marry in two years, and I don't see how to **pay for it**.
do: Ask Mr Nowak to let me take over **credit control**.
Plan a **small wedding** at the parish hall and keep clear of AI.
feel: **Peaceful** apart from the money, because work feels like belonging.
S0.quote: I'd rather start married with no new debt than have a big photo album.
fieldNote: Trust is **personal**: he'd rather ask a person than a program.
His real pressure is **debt and the wedding**, not technology.
A friend's essay with an invented source turned him off AI for good.

steps.text: Ask Mr Nowak to give me the credit control side
Plan a small wedding at the parish hall with Ola's family
Save 70 a month and pay the loan on time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's overdone but real. Some office jobs will be hit, and the answer is work and training, not waiting for handouts. I'd tell the lads at the warehouse that learning a trade or staying useful is the best protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. My job, invoices, chasing payments and reconciling the till, is the type that a program takes. The owner's son, Piotr, has already asked about software for the books. If Mr Nowak buys it, there's me and there's Mrs Zielinska who does the payroll, and one of us goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the software only if it arrives, and I'd learn it properly with a person next to me. I'd also ask to spend part of the week in the yard and on deliveries, because I want a job that isn't just paperwork. And I'd see if the church men's group has contacts in building and trade work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I feel like a man who's been handed a ladder and told it's the wrong wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about moving to the yard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, fine. My grandfather was a builder and I used to carry bricks for him as a kid. I'd rather earn less and be useful than sit at a desk waiting to be replaced. A man should work, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ola? What does she say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says I need to be ready to move. She's a nurse's aide, so her job isn't going anywhere. I tell her I'll find something, but I'm slow to make a move. She notices that.

say: It's overdone but real, and the answer is **work and training**, not handouts.
I'd tell the lads that staying **useful** is the best protection.
think: My invoices and payment chasing are the kind a **program** takes.
Piotr, the owner's son, has asked about **software for the books**.
do: Learn any new software **only if it arrives**, with a person beside me.
Spend part of the week in the **yard** and ask the church men's group about trade work.
feel: **Heavy**, like being handed a ladder against the wrong wall.
S1.quote: I'd rather earn less and be useful than sit at a desk waiting to be replaced.
fieldNote: Instinct is **work**, not benefits, in line with his traditional outlook.
Open to **hands-on** work, a family tradition through his grandfather.
Ola's job is stable, but he admits he's **slow** to move.

steps.text: Ask Mr Nowak to put me in the yard two days a week
Learn the books software only with a colleague checking my work
Ask the church men's group about building trade jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not a joke. It would break a lot of families. I'd tell people at church to look after each other, and I'd say the government must protect those who have worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd fear for my job and my marriage plans. If office work goes in two years, I'm one of the first to be let go, and I have a pass degree and debt. Ola and I would have to wait on the wedding. I'd feel I'd let her down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything extra and ask Mr Nowak to put me on deliveries or the yard now, before the software arrives. I'd go to my pastor and the men's group for work leads. If it came to it, I'd move into Ola's mother's spare room, which she's offered. I would not take handouts for long; I'd take any job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hollow feeling, like when the factory closed in my uncle's town. I remember what that did to the men.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your uncle's town.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was a small place, one big plant, and when it closed, half the men sat at home. Drink, arguments, the church hall full of food parcels. My uncle never worked again. I swore I'd never be the man my uncle became, and now I'm scared I might be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop that happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep moving. Do any work, even the worst. Stay close to Ola's family and the church. A man who's busy and has people around him doesn't fall as far.

say: Two years is no joke and would **break** a lot of families.
I'd tell people at church to **look after each other**.
think: If office work goes in two years, I'm among the **first let go**.
Ola and I would have to **wait on the wedding**, and I'd feel I'd let her down.
do: Stop extras and ask Mr Nowak for **deliveries or the yard** now.
Go to my pastor for **work leads**, and accept Ola's mother's offer of a spare room.
feel: A **hollow feeling**, remembering my uncle's town after the factory closed.
S2.quote: I swore I'd never be the man my uncle became, and now I'm scared I might be.
fieldNote: The **uncle's story** drives his fear of idleness.
Accepts **family and church** help but not long-term handouts.
Expects to lose his job and has debt, so **alarmed**.

steps.text: Stop all extras and the Friday football fees
Ask Mr Nowak for delivery and yard work now
Talk to my pastor about local work leads
Move into Ola's mother's spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we don't waste it. I'd say people should learn real skills, trades, care and farming, and keep their families close. I'd say it plainly at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels bearable. I'd be 27, maybe married, with the debt nearly gone. But I'm not quick to change, and I worry I'd put it off until the last year. I've always been better at holding on than letting go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year: take a part-time course in bricklaying or a construction qualification at the college. Pay the debt down by 100 a month. Marry Ola, with a small wedding. Ask Mr Nowak for more yard work and keep doing the books. I'd go for a trade that a robot takes longer to do, even if the pay starts low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two-year one. It feels like a rough road, but there's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bricklaying and not something with computers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not a computer person, and I don't pretend to be. I like seeing a wall go up. Robots come three years after the thinking machines, but a skilled man on a messy site is still worth a lot. I'll have my hands and a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you from doing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride about the degree. I spent three years on it, and it feels like throwing it away. My mother tells me the degree isn't wasted, it just isn't enough. I'm trying to believe her.

say: Five years is enough to get ready if we don't **waste it**.
People should learn **real skills** like trades and care, and keep families close.
think: Five years feels **bearable**: I'd be 27, maybe married, with the debt nearly gone.
I'm better at **holding on** than letting go, and might delay.
do: Take a part-time **bricklaying** course at the college and pay 100 a month off the debt.
Marry Ola in a **small wedding** and keep doing the books.
feel: **Better** than the two-year case: a rough road, but a path.
S3.quote: I like seeing a wall go up.
fieldNote: Chooses a **hands-on trade**, sensing robots come later for it.
Mother helps him accept that the **degree** isn't wasted.
Names his own habit of **delaying** change.

steps.text: Enrol on a part-time bricklaying course at the college
Pay 100 a month off the student debt
Hold a small wedding with Ola at the parish hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should use it. Families, churches and employers should help people train, and the government should keep out of the way except for the very poor. I'd also say people are wrong to be afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels almost comfortable. I'd be 32, married, maybe with a child, and the debt long gone. I'd have a trade as well as the degree. The part that bothers me is that I won't want to change until I have to, and ten years might make me lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the wholesaler for a few years, then train as a site supervisor or run a small builder's merchant myself. I'd save for a house in the town, not the city. I'd bring up my kids to value work and to ask people, not machines. I'd probably use some software when it's old enough that everyone trusts it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. It feels like the future I'd planned, with a few extra bolts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To work with their hands and their heads. To look after their grandparents. To not believe everything a machine tells them. I'd also teach them that a handshake counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who panics about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't sit alone. Go to church or the pub or the football pitch, and talk to somebody older who's seen bad times. Panic is worse alone than with people.

say: Ten years is long, so families and employers should **help people train**.
People are **wrong to be afraid** if they use the time.
think: Ten years feels **almost comfortable**: married, maybe a child and no debt at 32.
I won't want to change until I have to, and a decade might make me **lazy**.
do: Stay a few years, then train as a **site supervisor** or run my own merchant.
Save for a **house in the town** and use software once everyone trusts it.
feel: **Settled**, like the future I'd planned with a few extra bolts.
S4.quote: Panic is worse alone than with people.
fieldNote: Values **community and handshakes**, in line with his traditional outlook.
Mood is uneasy: his job looks safe, but he fears his own **inertia**.

steps.text: Train as a site supervisor while staying at the wholesaler
Save a house deposit in the home town
Raise children to work with their hands and ask people first
Plan to run a small builders' merchant by 2034

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's too quick for any family to cope with, and I'd lose my job, my plans for the wedding and my feeling of being useful. What would help is a real offer of work, even basic, and a place to retrain with an apprenticeship pay, not just a classroom. I'd also want my church and family to stay close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not stuck in the past. I just think work has dignity, and that families should hold each other up. If a machine does the work, somebody still needs to look after the people.

headlineQuote: I just think work has dignity, and that families should hold each other up. If a machine does the work, somebody still needs to look after the people.
portrait: Marco is a **22-year-old** accounts clerk at a family building-supplies wholesaler, renting a room and owing about twenty thousand.
He is traditional: church, a steady girlfriend, work over handouts and a **handshake** over a program.
He never uses AI, partly after a friend's essay cited an invented source.
His instinct is to move **towards hands-on work**, which fits his grandfather's builder background.
He goes from uneasy to **alarmed** in the two-year case, recalling what a factory closing did to his uncle's town.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would end his job and his wedding plans, and he fears becoming like his uncle.
whatWouldHelp: A real **offer of work**, apprenticeship pay for retraining, and church and family staying close.
